lesson.title: Crest Factor: Measuring How Peaky a Waveform Really Is
lesson.summary: Crest factor is the ratio of a waveform's peak value to its RMS value, and it tells you how far a signal spikes above the steady level that actually does work or delivers heating power.
lesson.body:
Peak value and RMS value each describe a waveform, but they answer different questions. Peak value tells you the single highest instantaneous value the signal ever reaches. RMS value tells you the equivalent steady, DC level that would deliver the same average power into a resistor. Two waveforms can share the exact same RMS value and still behave very differently in a real circuit if one of them spends most of its time near zero and only occasionally shoots up to a sharp spike. Crest factor is the number that captures that difference: it is defined simply as Crest Factor = Peak Value divided by RMS Value.

A pure sine wave with peak amplitude 10 V has an RMS value of 10 V divided by the square root of 2, which is about 0.707, giving RMS = 7.07 V. Dividing peak by RMS gives Crest Factor = 10 V / 7.07 V = 1.414, which is exactly the square root of 2. This is why the value 1.414 shows up so often in AC electronics: it is the crest factor of any sine wave, no matter its amplitude or frequency.

Now compare that to a narrow pulse train with the same 10 V peak, but which is only on for 10 percent of each period, a 10 percent duty cycle, and sits at 0 V the rest of the time. The RMS value of a rectangular pulse equals the peak value multiplied by the square root of the duty cycle, so RMS = 10 V times the square root of 0.1, which is 10 V times 0.316, or 3.16 V. The crest factor is then 10 V / 3.16 V = 3.16, more than double the sine wave's 1.414. Both waveforms could be delivering the same average heating power if their RMS values matched, but the pulse train demands a component, an amplifier, a power supply, a wire, that can survive a peak more than three times its RMS level, while the sine wave only ever peaks 1.414 times above its RMS.

This is exactly why audio amplifiers, power supplies, and instrumentation are rated with headroom above their continuous RMS rating. Music and speech have crest factors well above a sine wave's 1.414 because they contain sharp transients, drum hits, and consonants, and an amplifier that can only handle 1.414 times its rated RMS voltage will clip and distort every time a loud transient arrives. Engineers use crest factor to decide how much extra peak capability a circuit needs beyond what the RMS power rating alone would suggest.
